title: Inflated forecasts, consultants and insiders
summary:
The lenders' own reviews and two insiders document forecasts and lending pressure that ran ahead of reality. IMF staff economist Davison Budhoo resigned in 1988 saying the Fund had overstated Trinidad and Tobago's 1980-85 rise in real unit labour costs (164.7% against his 66.1%); a government committee (the Bourne Committee) found the IMF index even more inflated, and the IMF denied any error in a 20 March 1989 telex (Multinational Monitor, 1990). The World Bank's 1992 Wapenhans report found the share of Bank projects with major problems rose from 11% (FY1981) to 20% (FY1991) and tied this to an "approval culture" (World Bank IEG). In Pakistan, the March 1994 power policy assumed about 7% yearly demand growth and drew about 4,500 MW of private plants; the World Bank Group, which had advised a cap near 2,000 MW, was involved in 11 of 16 plants, and demand grew more slowly, leaving surplus capacity (Fraser, World Bank, 2005). Indonesia's Paiton private plant had a high take-or-pay share set against an over-optimistic demand projection (Yuliyanti, MIT, 2001) and was renegotiated after 1997.

IMF research finds growth forecasts in IMF-supported programs lean optimistic: Baqir, Ramcharan and Sahay (2005, 94 programs, 1989-2002) found a bias in growth and inflation forecasts, while an IMF evaluation paper (Luna, 2014, 103 programs, 2002-11) found only a weak bias overall, significant only in programs with exceptional access to Fund money. The US-Saudi Joint Commission (JECOR), set up in 1974 and run by the US Treasury with Saudi money, had placed about US$140 million in contracts with over 100 US firms by 1978 (GAO, 1979). John Perkins's 2004 memoir Confessions of an Economic Hit Man alleges a deliberate scheme of inflated forecasts at the Boston firm Chas. T. Main; its claims are listed below as one author's word. Records confirm only the outline of his career at Main; the crash inquiries in Panama and Ecuador found no sabotage, and the US State Department and his former colleagues disputed key parts.

countries.note: Seat of the IMF and World Bank (Washington) and home of Chas. T. Main (Boston), bought by Parsons of Pasadena in 1985 (Boston Magazine, 2006). The US Treasury ran JECOR, which by 1978 held US$250 million of Saudi deposits and had contracts with over 100 US firms worth about US$140 million (GAO, 1979).

The Paiton private power contract paid slightly over 8 US cents/kWh (Wikipedia, uncited); the state utility PLN sought to cancel or renegotiate it in 1999, and in July 2002 agreed a price slightly under 5 cents for part of the output (Wikipedia, citing Jakarta Post). An MIT thesis (Yuliyanti, 2001) finds a high take-or-pay share set against an over-optimistic demand projection. MIGA, a World Bank affiliate, gave guarantees (Wikipedia, citing MIGA).

The March 1994 power policy issued letters of support for 34 projects over 9,000 MW; 20 plants with about 4,500 MW reached financial close, on assumed demand growth near 7% a year. Demand grew more slowly and left excess capacity; the Bank Group had advised a cap near 2,000 MW and was involved in 11 of 16 plants (88% of private MW). In July 1998 the government alleged corruption against Hubco (1,292 MW, US$1.6 billion), which Hubco denied; a December 2000 settlement cut the tariff (Fraser, World Bank, 2005).

IMF staff economist Davison Budhoo, who worked on the 1985-87 missions, said the 1986 mission overstated the 1980-85 rise in real unit labour costs (164.7% against 66.1%). The government's Bourne Committee found the IMF index even more inflated; Kari Levitt upheld the substance but doubted it mattered much. The IMF denied error in a 20 March 1989 telex. Two loans of US$110.5 million each followed in 1989 and 1990, after a 15% devaluation and public wage cuts (Multinational Monitor, 1990).

The World Bank's own evaluation (Berney, OED, 2002) says early expectations of rapid reform were highly unrealistic; two oil rehabilitation loans of US$1.1 billion disbursed only US$760.5 million and were rated unsatisfactory.

Omar Torrijos died on 31 July 1981 when a Panamanian Air Force Twin Otter (FAP-205) hit Marta mountain near Coclesito (Aviation Safety Network). Experts found no explosive residue, and on 3 April 1983 a Penonomé judge provisionally closed the case, ruling out criminal involvement (La Estrella de Panamá, 2015). His brother Hugo said in 1986 he was 90% sure of a plot (same source). Perkins's claim is listed under one author's claims.

President Jaime Roldós died on 24 May 1981 when an Air Force Beechcraft King Air crashed in Loja. Inquiries at the time found a navigation error and ruled out sabotage (El Comercio; Wikipedia, citing UPI). A 1990-92 inquiry found gaps but no conclusion, and the case was reopened in 2013 (Wikipedia, citing El Telégrafo). Perkins's claim is listed under one author's claims.

The US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation (JECOR) was set up on 8 June 1974; by 30 September 1978 Saudi Arabia had deposited US$250 million in a Treasury trust account, and over 100 US firms held contracts worth about US$140 million (GAO, 1979). Saudi funding meant no US appropriation or congressional oversight was needed; the commission ran until about 2001 (Middle East Institute, 2009).

timeline.event: John Perkins, 26, joins Chas. T. Main in Boston as a junior economist.
The US and Saudi Arabia set up JECOR on 8 June, a Treasury-run program paid for by Saudi deposits.

Ecuador's President Jaime Roldós dies in a plane crash in Loja on 24 May; inquiries find a navigation error and rule out sabotage.

IMF economist Davison Budhoo resigns with a public letter of over 100 pages alleging deliberate statistical errors.

A World Bank review of about 300 power projects financed 1965-83 finds declining power-sector performance.
The Wapenhans report finds projects with major problems rose from 11% (FY1981) to 20% (FY1991) and cites an approval culture.
Ecuador's Granda inquiry into the Roldós crash issues a 26-volume report with inconsistencies but no conclusion.
Pakistan's March 1994 power policy issues letters of support for 34 private projects over 9,000 MW.
The US GAO reports the Bank's own task force blamed a culture focused on loan approval and disbursement.
In July Pakistan issues nine termination notices to private power plants holding about two-thirds of contracted capacity, seven citing corruption.
Indonesia's PLN agrees a price slightly under 5 US cents/kWh for part of Paiton's output, down from slightly over 8 (per Wikipedia).
Baqir, Ramcharan and Sahay (IMF Staff Papers) find optimistic growth and inflation forecasts in 94 programs, 1989-2002 (as reviewed by Luna, 2014).

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says the National Security Agency tested and screened him before Chas. T. Main hired him (ch. 1).
claims_per_author.status: Unconfirmed. Einar Greve, who recruited him, told Boston Magazine (2006) he knew no one at the NSA. A State Department statement (2 February 2006) reportedly found no documentary or testimonial evidence and said the NSA has no economic mission; that statement and a New York Times review that found no evidence for the NSA claims are known here only through Wikipedia.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says Main vice president Einar Greve recruited him (ch. 1).
claims_per_author.status: Confirmed in outline: Greve says he recruited Perkins and told the Tucson Citizen the story was basically true, but disputes where they met, the NSA link and the Ecuador letters (Boston Magazine 2006).

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says a Main consultant, Claudine Martin, trained him as an economic hit man whose job was to win big loans that would flow back to US firms (ch. 2).
claims_per_author.status: Unconfirmed. Greve called the seduction episode fiction; Perkins told Boston Magazine (2006) he came to doubt the name on her card was real, and the magazine described his supporting evidence as flimsy.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says such loans were meant to send money back to Main and to Bechtel, Halliburton, Stone & Webster and Brown & Root (ch. 2).
claims_per_author.status: No project record linking these firms to Main forecasts was found. Boston Magazine (2006) separately reports a US$200 million Bechtel bribe to a Saudi prince over the Riyadh airport contract in the late 1970s, without giving a source; it is not confirmed here.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says Main expected Java electricity forecasts of at least 17% yearly growth; that senior forecaster Howard Parker said no load had grown over 7-9% a year for long and 6% was more reasonable (ch. 5); and that Parker was fired over an 8% forecast, after which Perkins produced 17-19% forecasts (ch. 9).
claims_per_author.status: Unconfirmed. Boston Magazine (2006) retells the Parker firing from Perkins's account. No Main forecast documents were found: the Northeastern University archive of Main records covers 1975-77 and names no Indonesian work, and a Parsons spokeswoman said she did not know where Main's records would be.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says he helped design a plan to recycle Saudi oil money into US-built modernization (ch. 15).
claims_per_author.status: The structure is real: JECOR, created in 1974, held US$250 million of Saudi deposits by 1978 and placed about US$140 million in contracts with US firms (GAO 1979). No record found shows Perkins's personal role.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says Omar Torrijos was assassinated by "CIA-sanctioned jackals" (Preface, p. ix), and in ch. 27 (pp. 158-159) cites Graham Greene quoting Torrijos's guard that there was a bomb on the plane.
claims_per_author.status: Not supported by the record found. Experts found no explosive residue, and a judge provisionally closed the case in April 1983, ruling out criminal involvement; a De Havilland expert reportedly did not rule out foul play, and Torrijos's brother alleged a plot in 1986 (La Estrella de Panamá, 2015). Wikipedia says, without citation, that the case was later declared unsolved and that files went missing during the 1989 US invasion.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says Jaime Roldós was assassinated for opposing foreign oil interests (Preface, p. ix; ch. 26, pp. 153-157, citing eyewitness claims that a decoy plane blew up).
claims_per_author.status: Contradicted by the 1981 inquiries, which found a navigation error and ruled out sabotage (El Comercio; Wikipedia, citing UPI). A 1990-92 inquiry found gaps but no conclusion, and the case was reopened in 2013 after a documentary alleged Operation Condor involvement (Wikipedia, citing El Telégrafo).

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says that where economic hit men failed, CIA-linked jackals stepped in, as in Iraq and Venezuela (Preface; Prologue; ch. 31, 33).
claims_per_author.status: No record found to confirm or test this.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says he was promoted to Chief Economist at Main (ch. 9) and later quit out of conscience (ch. 25).
claims_per_author.status: A New York Times review found the arc of his career accurately described (known here only through Wikipedia). Boston Magazine (2006) confirms he joined as a junior economist in 1971; his former supervisor Frank Fullerton said he left because he thought he was worth more.

claims_per_author.author: Joseph Stiglitz
claims_per_author.work: New Republic essay on the world economic crisis (17 April 2000)
claims_per_author.claim: Stiglitz, World Bank chief economist from 1996 to November 1999, says the IMF and US Treasury applied austerity and high interest rates to East Asia in 1997-98 when the problem was private debt, deepening the downturn; that Thailand, which followed IMF advice most closely, did worse than Malaysia and South Korea; and that Treasury pushed financial liberalization in Korea in 1993.
claims_per_author.status: One insider's account. The IMF's response is not in the sources checked. The 2014 IMF evaluation paper on forecasts does not test these claims.

claims_per_author.author: Joseph Stiglitz
claims_per_author.work: New Republic essay on the world economic crisis (17 April 2000)
claims_per_author.claim: Stiglitz says the IMF pressed Indonesia to cut spending so that subsidies for food and fuel were eliminated just when they were most needed.
claims_per_author.status: Partly supported for fuel: Indonesia's January 1998 letter of intent to the IMF committed to phase out fuel and electricity subsidies gradually from 1 April 1998, keeping kerosene and diesel rises small to protect the poor. Food subsidies are not in that letter.

claims_per_author.author: Joseph Stiglitz
claims_per_author.work: New Republic essay on the world economic crisis (17 April 2000)
claims_per_author.claim: Stiglitz says the rapid privatization urged on Russia by the IMF and Treasury let a small group of oligarchs take state assets.
claims_per_author.status: One insider's view. The World Bank's own evaluation (Berney, OED, 2002) says early hopes for rapid reform were highly unrealistic but does not address this claim.

claims_per_author.author: Davison Budhoo
claims_per_author.work: Enough Is Enough, open letter to Michel Camdessus (1988)
claims_per_author.claim: Budhoo says the IMF used deliberate statistical fraud to impose policies on Trinidad and Tobago and other countries.
claims_per_author.status: For Trinidad's unit labour cost figure, the government's Bourne Committee found the IMF index even more inflated, and the Levitt investigation upheld the substance; the IMF denied any error (Multinational Monitor 1990). His wider claim of systematic fraud elsewhere is not confirmed.

uncertain: No record found shows what Chas. T. Main actually forecast or built in Indonesia, Panama, Ecuador, Colombia, Iran or Saudi Arabia; the firm's surviving archive at Northeastern covers 1975-77 and names Turkey and the Jordan Valley among its foreign work.

Whether anyone caused the 1981 deaths of Torrijos and Roldós is unproven; the inquiries found no sabotage, later Ecuadorian inquiries reached no conclusion partly because the plane had no black box, and Torrijos's family alleged a plot.

Critics dispute Perkins's whole thesis: Sebastian Mallaby (Washington Post) called his basic contentions wrong, and Niall Ferguson (2008) noted US loans to Ecuador and Panama were too small a share to kill for (both known here only through Wikipedia).

The State Department statement "Confessions - or Fantasies - of an Economic Hit Man?" is dated 2 February 2006 in Wikipedia's citation; its text could not be reached and is known here only through Wikipedia.

IMF growth-forecast optimism is contested: Baqir, Ramcharan and Sahay (2005, 94 programs 1989-2002) found a bias that survived controls, while Luna (2014, 103 programs 2002-11) found it weak overall and significant only in exceptional-access programs.

Whether Pakistan's 1994 private-power surplus came from inflated forecasts or from slower growth is not settled; the World Bank paper says demand grew more slowly than the roughly 7% assumed but does not measure the forecast error.
Paiton's original price of slightly over 8 US cents/kWh is uncited in Wikipedia and was not checked against the contract.

The Multinational Monitor account reports no IMF review of Budhoo's charges beyond the 1989 denial; the IMF later dropped the disputed index for the real effective exchange rate, citing comparability with other countries.

dropped.idea: Main's documented projects in Indonesia, Panama, Ecuador, Colombia and Saudi Arabia
dropped.why: No archive or World Bank record naming Main in these countries was found; two World Bank archive files checked did not mention Main.
Only the chapter title (ch. 21) was read; no record of a Main project in Colombia was found.

dropped.idea: Stone & Webster, Halliburton and Bechtel project links
dropped.why: No primary record tying these firms to forecast-driven loans was found; only a reported, unconfirmed Bechtel bribe allegation.

dropped.idea: World Bank Operations Evaluation findings on over-optimistic demand forecasts
dropped.why: No OED report stating this was opened; the 1989 power lending review abstract shows declining performance but does not mention forecasts.

dropped.idea: New York Times review and State Department statement on Perkins in full
dropped.why: Archived copies could not be reached; their findings are reported only through Wikipedia.
Perkins writes about Iran (ch. 18), but Boston Magazine mentions Iran work without naming a Main project, and no record was found.

dropped.idea: Thailand and South Korea as forecast cases
dropped.why: Their only part in this layer was Stiglitz's account, which is kept as his claim.

dropped.idea: Stiglitz's remark that IMF staff are often third-rank students from first-rate universities
dropped.why: The phrase is in his 2000 essay, but it is an opinion about staff, not a documented part of the pattern.

check_note: All cited pages were checked except the Perkins book scan, which was read in full text. Perkins and Stiglitz accounts were taken out of the summary, country notes, links and timeline and kept as their claims; Thailand, South Korea and Iran were removed because their only link was one author's word, and the Stiglitz timeline entry and Perkins and Stiglitz map lines were removed. Torrijos crash facts were moved off uncited Wikipedia text to Aviation Safety Network and La Estrella de Panamá (1983 court closure, not a ruling on pilot error); Roldós inquiry findings now cite El Comercio. Fixed Perkins page and chapter references (Torrijos is Preface and ch. 27, pp. 158-159; Parker firing is ch. 9), the Parsons records remark, Boston Magazine's wording (flimsy evidence), Wapenhans fiscal years, JECOR end date (about 2001), Hubco's denial, and the IEO wording on exceptional-access programs. Added Indonesia's 1998 IMF letter of intent to test Stiglitz's subsidy claim. Points that rest only on Wikipedia (State Department statement, New York Times review, Mallaby, Ferguson, Paiton price) are now marked as such.

title: The economists' pipeline
summary:
US universities, foundations and aid agencies trained economists from borrowing countries who later ran finance ministries, central banks and planning agencies while those countries took IMF and World Bank programs. In March 1956 Chile's Catholic University signed a cooperation agreement with the University of Chicago, paid for with US government funds (Stabili, 2021); about 100 Chileans trained between 1957 and 1970 (Wikipedia). After the 1973 coup they held the economy, finance, planning and labour ministries (Sergio de Castro, finance 1977-82; Hernán Büchi, finance 1985-89). A 1975 US Senate staff report says CIA project files record that CIA collaborators helped prepare the junta's first overall economic plan, without naming the authors. In Indonesia the Ford Foundation sent University of Indonesia students to UC Berkeley from 1957; after 1966 this group ran planning (Widjojo Nitisastro, Bappenas 1967-83) and finance (Ali Wardhana, 1968-83), and Widjojo led delegations to the IMF, World Bank and the aid group IGGI.

From the 1980s, US-based advisers worked inside governments. Harvard's Jeffrey Sachs advised Bolivia in 1985, Poland in 1989-90 and Russia's Yeltsin government from late 1991 to January 1994 (IMF Finance & Development, 2012); Bolivian writers dispute that he helped draft Bolivia's August 1985 stabilization decree. USAID gave Harvard's Institute for International Development (HIID) a noncompetitive award for Russia in December 1992 that grew to US$40.4 million (GAO 1996); the US government sued, and in 2005 Harvard agreed to pay US$26.5 million, Andrei Shleifer US$2 million and Jonathan Hay up to US$2 million, without admitting liability, after a 2004 ruling that Shleifer and Hay broke conflict-of-interest rules. In 1989 John Williamson listed ten reforms with support among experts at the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury, which he called the Washington Consensus. Mexico's cabinet under Carlos Salinas (Harvard) included Pedro Aspe (MIT), Ernesto Zedillo (Yale) and Jaime Serra Puche (Yale, Stanford); Argentina's Domingo Cavallo (Harvard PhD 1977) ran the 1991 convertibility plan.

countries.note: University of Chicago (Chile agreement from 1956), UC Berkeley with Ford Foundation funds (Indonesia, from 1957), Harvard (Sachs; HIID's US$40.4 million USAID Russia award), MIT and Yale (Mexican ministers), and Williamson's 1989 Washington Consensus list.

The Catholic University-Chicago agreement was signed in March 1956 with US government funds (Stabili 2021); about 100 economists trained 1957-70 (Wikipedia). Under Pinochet they held finance (de Castro 1977-82; Büchi 1985-89), economy (Baraona 1976-79), labour and pensions (Piñera 1978-80), and planning, labour and the central bank (Kast). Their program El Ladrillo was finished weeks before the 1973 coup; a 1975 Senate staff report says CIA collaborators helped prepare the junta's first economic plan.

Ford Foundation-backed Berkeley training began in 1957. After an August 1966 seminar, Suharto announced a stabilization program on 3 October 1966; inflation fell from 650% (1966) to 13% (1969) (Wikipedia). Widjojo headed Bappenas 1967-83 and led IGGI, Paris Club, IMF and World Bank delegations; Ali Wardhana (Berkeley PhD 1962) was finance minister 1968-83; Mohammad Sadli (MIT, Berkeley) was first head of the investment board in 1967.

Reason (1989) lists President Salinas (Harvard), Treasury Secretary Pedro Aspe (MIT doctorate, a lead backer of privatization), Budget Secretary Ernesto Zedillo (Yale doctorate) and Commerce Secretary Jaime Serra Puche (Yale, Stanford). Sarah Babb's Managing Mexico (Princeton, 2001) traces how US-credentialed economists came to dominate policymaking.

Domingo Cavallo, Harvard PhD 1977, headed the central bank in 1982, was economy minister 1991-96 and introduced the 1991 dollar-pegged convertibility plan; he returned in 2001 and resigned on 19 December 2001 after the corralito deposit freeze (Group of Thirty; Biografías y Vidas). Wikipedia also lists Chicago-trained Adolfo Diz and Roque Fernández.

Sachs was an economic adviser to Bolivia from 1985, when annual inflation was about 60,000%; by early 1986 the hyperinflation was over, and he negotiated a debt deal that cancelled 90% of external debt on the books (IMF F&D, 2012). Decree 21060 of 29 August 1985 under President Paz Estenssoro froze wages; Bolivian writers say a team led by Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada drafted it, not Sachs (Laserna, Los Tiempos, 2025).

Poland's government approached Sachs in early 1989; he and David Lipton drafted a plan with Solidarity leaders, and Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz led the plan launched on 1 January 1990. Sachs told Solidarity the foreign debt would be cancelled (IMF Finance & Development, 2012).

Sachs advised Yeltsin's government from late 1991 to January 1994 (IMF F&D, 2012). HIID received about US$40 million of USAID's US$325 million Russian privatization program (FY1992-96), helped create the Russian Privatization Center and was principal drafter of 3 of 9 core laws (GAO 1996). A US court found Shleifer and Hay liable under the False Claims Act in 2004; the 2005 settlements totalled at least US$31 million.

USAID gave HIID a noncompetitive US$1.5 million award in May 1996, scaled back from a proposal of about US$6 million, on foreign policy grounds after Ukrainian officials asked for HIID; GAO noted possible duplication with other donors (GAO 1996).

timeline.event: Chile's Catholic University and the University of Chicago sign a scientific cooperation agreement in March, with US government funds.
Ford Foundation-funded training of University of Indonesia economists at UC Berkeley begins.
Ali Wardhana completes his Berkeley PhD on monetary policy in Indonesia.
Suharto announces a stabilization program on 3 October based partly on the University of Indonesia economists' advice.
Widjojo Nitisastro becomes head of Indonesia's planning agency Bappenas, a post held until 1983.
Berkeley-trained Ali Wardhana becomes Indonesia's finance minister, serving until 1983.
Chicago-trained economists finish El Ladrillo, an economic program, weeks before the 11 September coup in Chile.
Milton Friedman visits Chile from 20 to 27 March and meets Pinochet on 21 March.
A US Senate staff report of 18 December says CIA project files record that CIA collaborators helped prepare the junta's first economic plan.
Sergio de Castro becomes Chile's finance minister, serving to 1982.
Bolivia issues Decree 21060 on 29 August under President Paz Estenssoro; Sachs advises the government, though his role in drafting it is disputed.
John Williamson lists ten reforms with support among experts at the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury and calls them the Washington Consensus.
Mexico's new cabinet includes US-trained Salinas, Aspe, Zedillo and Serra Puche.
Poland launches its economic plan on 1 January, led by Balcerowicz and drafted with Sachs and Lipton.
Harvard-trained Domingo Cavallo becomes Argentina's economy minister and introduces the convertibility plan.
USAID makes a noncompetitive award to Harvard's HIID for Russia in December; it grows to US$40.4 million by September 1995.
The US GAO reports minimal USAID oversight of HIID's legal reform work in Russia.
Cavallo resigns as Argentina's economy minister on 19 December after the deposit freeze.
Judge Douglas Woodlock finds Shleifer and Hay liable under the False Claims Act; Harvard is liable for breach of contract.
Harvard agrees to pay US$26.5 million, Shleifer US$2 million and Hay up to US$2 million, admitting no liability.

claims_per_author.author: Joseph Stiglitz
claims_per_author.work: New Republic essay on the world economic crisis (17 April 2000)
claims_per_author.claim: Stiglitz says Russia's rapid privatization and capital opening, urged by the IMF and US Treasury, let oligarchs take state assets, and that poverty rose to almost 50%.
claims_per_author.status: One insider's view. The World Bank's OED (2002) separately says early expectations of rapid reform in Russia were highly unrealistic. GAO (1996) did not assess privatization outcomes; it found the Privatization Center's privatization support generally successful.

claims_per_author.author: Milton and Rose Friedman
claims_per_author.work: Two Lucky People (memoir, 1998), as cited by Wikipedia
claims_per_author.claim: The Friedmans say Pinochet turned to the Chicago-trained economists in 1975, when inflation still raged, and gave several of them powerful posts.
claims_per_author.status: Known here only through Wikipedia's citation (p. 398). Consistent with the documented appointments (Baraona, economy, 1976-79; de Castro, finance, 1977-82).

claims_per_author.author: Andrei Shleifer and Harvard
claims_per_author.work: Statements on the 2005 settlement (Harvard Magazine; Harvard Crimson)
claims_per_author.claim: Harvard says the court affirmed it engaged in no institutional wrongdoing; Shleifer says he settled without admitting liability because his legal fees would have exceeded the payment.
claims_per_author.status: The court had already found Shleifer and Hay liable in June 2004 and Harvard liable for breach of contract, while clearing Harvard of knowing fraud; the settlement contains no admission (Harvard Magazine; Harvard Crimson).

claims_per_author.author: Jeffrey Sachs
claims_per_author.work: Accounts in interviews and The End of Poverty (2005), as reported by Laserna (Los Tiempos, 2025) and IMF F&D (2012)
claims_per_author.claim: Sachs presents Bolivia's 1985 stabilization as largely his work, with ending fuel subsidies as the key step.
claims_per_author.status: Disputed. Laserna says a Bolivian team led by Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada drafted Decree 21060 and no one from Harvard took part; IMF F&D (2012) confirms Sachs was an adviser from 1985.

uncertain: The Church Committee staff report says the CIA funded over 75% of an opposition research organization in 1973 and that CIA collaborators helped prepare the junta's first economic plan; it does not name the organization, El Ladrillo or the Chicago-trained economists, so the link between the two is not established.
El Ladrillo's date is reported differently: Wikipedia's Chicago Boys page gives 1969 for an earlier program; the El ladrillo page and Edwards (via Econlib) place the final text in 1972-73.

Bolivia's peak inflation is given as about 60,000% (IMF F&D), 20,000 with no unit (Wikipedia) and over 8,000% (Chávez, eju.tv, 2025). Wikipedia's figures of a 93% devaluation and US$57 million of IMF credit are uncited and were not used.
Whether foreign training caused these policies or local politics did is argued, not settled; Babb (2001) stresses that national circumstances shape what economists do.
The link between Sachs's Harvard work and HIID's USAID Russia contract is not shown in the sources checked; the part of GAO 1996 read does not name Anatoly Chubais.
Mexican ministers' degrees come from one magazine article (Reason, 1989) plus Babb's general finding; individual degree records were not checked.
The figure of about 100 Chilean trainees (1957-70) rests on Wikipedia; Stabili's abstract says the advanced training programs ran until 1964.

check_note: All cited pages were checked. The Church Committee staff report was read further than before: it says CIA collaborators helped prepare the junta's first economic plan, now added with the caveat that it names no authors. Bolivia was corrected: Sachs's role in drafting Decree 21060 is disputed by Bolivian writers, and Wikipedia's uncited US$57 million IMF credit, 93% devaluation and 20,000% inflation were dropped; Sachs's own account moved to claims. The 1975 Friedman entry no longer says Pinochet then gave posts, which the review cited does not say. Fixed the Shleifer statement (he did not say he would have won), the Washington Consensus wording (support among experts, per PIIE), the HIID figure (US$40.4 million), the 75% CIA funding year (1973) and Chile's trainee count source (Wikipedia, not Stabili). Stiglitz's essay was removed from the confirming sources and kept as his claim.
